postData.title: Contributing to Next.js: What I Learned
postData.content:
# Contributing to Next.js: What I Learned

> A contribution to [Vercel/Next.js](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js>) addressing [Issue #96241](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/96241>).

## Overview

This contribution request was to add a startup warning to the Next.js development server when the printed **Network URL** may be inaccessible because of cross-origin restrictions.

- **Issue:** [#96241](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/96241>)
- **Pull Request:** #96283
- **Repository:** [vercel/next.js](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js>)

License Note: Next.js is released under the [MIT License](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/license.md>), an OSI-approved open-source license.

The primary purpose of the PR is to address an existing bug reported by another developer, **mhverbakel**, in [Issue #96241](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/96241>).

---

## What Changed?

When running Next.js in development mode, `next dev` prints two URLs:

```
Local:   http://localhost:3000
Network: http://192.168.1.2:3000
```

Before this change, attempting to access the Network URL could fail because of Next.js' cross-origin restrictions.

The behavior could be confusing because:

- The Network URL was displayed normally.
- The page could fail to load when accessed through that URL.
- HMR would not function correctly.
- The relevant warning was only visible later in the browser console.
- The terminal output did not immediately explain the problem or its solution.

## The Fix

My PR adds a warning directly to the development server's startup output.

The warning appears immediately after the Network URL is printed and explains:

- Why the Network URL may not work.
- That cross-origin access is restricted by default.
- That `allowedDevOrigins` can be configured to permit the required origin.

### Implementation

The change was limited to a single file:

```
packages/next/src/server/lib/app-info-log.ts
```

I added a `logAllowedDevOriginsInfo` function inside `logStartInfo` and called it immediately after the Network URL is logged.

Conceptually, the startup flow now looks like:

```
Start Next.js development server
      ↓
Print Local URL
      ↓
Print Network URL
      ↓
Print allowedDevOrigins information
```

This puts the explanation next to the Network URL instead of requiring the developer to discover the problem through the browser console.

---

## Course Context

This contribution was built on knowledge and experience developed throughout **OSU's CS 464**.

Two assignments were particularly relevant:

- **Report: Testing Methodology and Results**
- **Open or Claim an Issue and Submit the Link**

### Testing Methodology and Results

The Next.js page I reviewed for the Testing Methodology and Results assignment was not directly related to this PR. However, the assignment introduced me to the structure of the Next.js repository and gave me experience working with **TypeScript**.

Before taking CS 464, I had no previous experience with TypeScript or Next.js. The earlier code review therefore gave me useful background when navigating the repository for this contribution.

### Open or Claim an Issue

The Issue Link assignment had a more direct impact on this PR.

Through that assignment, I learned about:

- Next.js contribution guidelines
- Building the Next.js repository
- Running Next.js in different modes
- Creating and running tests
- Finding relevant files in the repository
- The process for opening and submitting a pull request

Because I had already worked with the repository during the earlier assignment, I had a better idea of where to begin investigating this issue.

For this PR, I knew that the problem was related to the development server and was therefore able to narrow my investigation toward the relevant server-side files.

---

## Contribution Process

### 1\. Finding an Existing Issue

I chose to work on an existing issue rather than creating a new issue.

Before starting work on [#96241](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/96241>), I checked the issue's comments to make sure that another contributor had not already claimed it.

At the time I began working on it, no contributor other than the original poster had claimed the issue.

### 2\. Reproducing the Issue

I first reproduced the reported behavior locally and confirmed that the Network URL could not be used as expected without additional configuration.

I then communicated with the original issue author, letting them know that I was able to reproduce the problem and intended to investigate a solution.

### 3\. Investigating the Proposed Fix

The issue initially suggested allowing `networkHostname` to work without requiring users to configure `allowedDevOrigins`.

While investigating the source code, I found the existing [`allowedDevOrigins` documentation](<https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/allowedDevOrigins>).

The documentation clarified that the current behavior was intentional.

Because of this, I changed my approach. Rather than changing the existing security behavior, I implemented the alternative solution described in the issue: **improve the developer-facing messaging**.

The resulting change explains to developers why the Network URL is restricted and points them toward the configuration required to use it.

---

## Following Project Guidelines

I also followed the contribution process documented by the Next.js project.

### Contribution Guide

The [Next.js contribution guide](<https://nextjs.org/docs/community/contribution-guide>) recommends that contributors understand GitHub's open-source contribution practices.

I followed this process by:

- Finding an existing issue.
- Checking whether another contributor was already working on it.
- Communicating with the issue author.
- Investigating the existing implementation and documentation.
- Searching for related pull requests.
- Following the repository's contribution requirements.

### `contributing.md`

The Next.js repository also contains a [`contributing.md`](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/contributing.md>) file describing project-specific contribution procedures.

The guide recommends checking existing issues and pull requests before beginning work. I searched existing PRs to ensure that there was not already a contribution addressing Issue #96241 or the same underlying problem.

I also watched the project's contribution walkthrough, **“How to Contribute to Open Source (Next.js)”**, which explains the expected contribution workflow.

---

## Commit Signing

The Next.js contribution guide requires commits targeting protected branches to be signed using a GitHub-verified:

- GPG key
- SSH key
- S/MIME key

Since my PR targeted changes related to the protected `canary` branch, I configured **SSH commit signing** for my GitHub account.

This allowed my commits to satisfy the repository's signed-commit requirements.

---

## Pull Request

Next.js provides different PR templates depending on the type of contribution.

Because this was a bug fix, I structured my PR around three questions:

```
What changed?
Why was it changed?
How was it changed?
```

The PR explains the reported problem, the reasoning behind the solution, and the specific implementation used to address it.

**PR:** #96283

---

## Validation

Before submitting the PR, I ran the formatting and linting commands recommended by the project:

```
pnpm prettier-fix
pnpm lint-fix
```

The PR successfully passed the automated checks configured by the Next.js repository.

At the time of writing, the remaining requirement for merging is **review and approval from a member of the Next.js team**.

---

## References

- mhverbakel. “[Network URL shown at startup is not accessible without allowedDevOrigins.](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/96241>)” _GitHub Issues_, Vercel/next.js, Issue #96241. Accessed July 2026.
- “[Next.js](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js>).” _GitHub_. Accessed July 27, 2026.
- “[Next.js](<https://nextjs.org/>).” _Next.js_. Accessed July 27, 2026.

> **Note:** Most sources I referenced for this were pages within the official Next.js website and their GitHub repository. To avoid repeating the same project in the references, only the primary website and repository are listed above.
